title: Check the rights review status and permitted uses together using “and”
reading_goal: and Read the flow that ensures the operation is available only when it satisfies both the permission review status and the permitted usage conditions.
question: What is required for `can_use` to be True?
choices: The rights status must be “reviewed,” and “intended_use” must also be on the allowlist.
It is sufficient for only one of the two conditions to be True.
You do not need to check the `rights_status` value.
answer: The rights status must be “reviewed,” and “intended_use” must also be on the allowlist.
explanation: 1) Compare `rights_status` with `reviewed`. 2) Check if the left-hand condition is True. 3) Check if `intended_use` is included in `allowed_uses`. 4) Since both conditions are True, `can_use` becomes True.
project_context: Use this combination of conditions when configuring an automatic gate before reusing external documents or data in learning content.
reading_goal_internal: and 연산이 권리 검토 상태와 허용 용도 조건을 모두 만족해야 사용 가능하게 만드는 흐름을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `and` A boolean operation sets the result to True only when both conditions are True.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It reads: "Check the permission status on the left, and if it is True, check the allowed membership on the right."
concept_explanation.key_point: When determining copyright and data governance, one must verify not only the existence of a source but also the status of rights and the actual terms of use.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: Do not conclude that a `reviewed` marker alone permits use for any purpose. Allowed-use conditions are separate.

teaching_example.code:
reviewed = True
allowed = False
can_publish = reviewed and allowed
print(can_publish)
teaching_example.walkthrough: Even if the first condition is True, the second is False, so the overall result of the "and" operation is False.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Compare `rights_status` with `reviewed`. 2) Check if the left-hand condition is True. 3) Check if `intended_use` is included in `allowed_uses`. 4) Since both conditions are True, `can_use` becomes True.
answer_explanation.why_correct: When determining copyright and data governance, one must verify not only the existence of a source but also the status of rights and the actual terms of use.

common_wrong_choice.choice: It is sufficient for only one of the two conditions to be True.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: That rule is similar to "or," while "and" requires both conditions to be True.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: First, check whether the boolean operator is “and” or “or.”

answer_explanation.takeaway: It accurately interprets the way conditions are combined, such as **“under review AND meets usage conditions”**, to determine the availability of rights.

The source display code is interpreted as **retrieve source field → pass to function → return display string**.
project_context: It is linked to a UI that displays source names and links on the learning cards so that users can verify the references.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: `function(a, b)` is a function call that passes two argument values to the function and receives a return value.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Calculate the actual values of each argument expression from left to right, then check the function’s return value.
concept_explanation.key_point: "Attribution" is information that allows users to verify the source of a card’s evidence.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that only the URL is passed to the function. The code actually has two arguments: the source name and the URL.

teaching_example.walkthrough: Two dict values are passed to the function, which generates the string ``Docs </docs>``.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: It retrieves two values from the `card` and passes them to the function in order. The function returns a string in the format `name | url`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the two positional arguments of the function call correspond to the `name` and `url` parameters, respectively.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: Function return values include not only names but also URLs.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where the combination of the second argument and the return string was omitted.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The source display code reads as **look up the source field → pass to a function → return a display string**.

title: Removing excluded data using filtered list comprehension
reading_goal: Read the comprehension that compares the status of each item and leaves only those that are not excluded in `usable_items`.
code:
items = [
    {"id": "a", "status": "ready"},
    {"id": "b", "status": "excluded"},
    {"id": "c", "status": "hold"},
]
usable_items = [item for item in items if item["status"] != "excluded"]
question: What is the ID stored in `usable_items`?
explanation: `ready` and `hold` are not `excluded`, so the condition is True for them. Only `b`, whose status is `excluded`, is filtered out. A filtered list comprehension includes only items whose condition is True. A tempting wrong answer is “only b,” which would correspond to `== "excluded"`. The mistake is reading `!=` in the opposite direction. In filter code, **check the comparison operator direction exactly**.
project_context: This ties into the process of removing excluded materials—those that do not meet usage conditions or have unclear sources—from the pool of actual content candidates.
reading_goal_internal: 각 item의 status를 비교해 excluded가 아닌 항목만 usable_items에 남기는 comprehension을 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A filtered list comprehension iterates through a list and collects only the items that satisfy a condition into a new list.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Check the iteration target and the condition following ``if``, and calculate the condition for each item.
concept_explanation.key_point: Since `!= "excluded"`, all statuses other than "excluded" remain.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easier to read `!=` as `==`. Currently, the task is not to select items that are excluded, but to exclude them.

teaching_example.code:
rows = [{"state": "ok"}, {"state": "blocked"}]
usable = [row for row in rows if row["state"] != "blocked"]
teaching_example.walkthrough: Only the "ok row" passes the criteria and remains in the "usable" category.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: Since `ready` and `hold` are not `excluded`, the condition is True. Only `b` is excluded because its status is `excluded`.
answer_explanation.why_correct: A filtered list comprehension includes only those items for which the condition is True in the result.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: The result applies when the condition ``== "excluded"`` is met.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of misreading `!=`.

answer_explanation.takeaway: The filter code must **accurately verify the direction of comparison operators**.

target_statement: usable_items = [item for item in items if item["status"] != "excluded"]
focus_span: [item for item in items if item["status"] != "excluded"]

title: Audit only materials missing a license or source URL
reading_goal: Create a collection for auditing by filtering out items that lack source/license metadata for each resource.
code:
items = [
    {"id": "a", "license": "CC-BY", "source_url": "https://example.test/a"},
    {"id": "b", "license": "", "source_url": "https://example.test/b"},
    {"id": "c", "license": "CC0", "source_url": ""},
]
missing = [item for item in items if not item.get("license") or not item.get("source_url")]
question: What are the typical issues identified during a license audit?
choices: Materials missing source URLs or license information
answer: Materials missing source URLs or license information
explanation: The “comprehension” selects items where either “license” or “source_url” is falsy. This is because the audit condition directly expresses the absence of rights/provenance metadata. Common misconception: To hide verification results, an audit is a check designed to reveal omissions rather than conceal them. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when the purpose of a governance audit is misunderstood. A license audit verifies the **simultaneous presence of source identity and rights/license metadata**.
project_context: It is linked to a quality gate that audits the source, license, and submission basis of the learning app data before publication.
reading_goal_internal: 자료별 source/license metadata 누락을 조건으로 걸러 audit 대상 collection을 만든다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: A filtered list comprehension puts only items satisfying the condition into a new list.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: It checks whether `not license or not source_url` becomes True when either value is missing.
concept_explanation.key_point: In data governance, it is necessary to identify data with missing source and usage rights/license information before publishing it.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It is easy to assume that if a source URL is provided, usage rights are automatically verified even if no license information is included.

answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because the "audit condition" directly refers to the absence of rights/provenance metadata.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: An audit is an inspection designed to reveal, rather than conceal, omissions.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example of misunderstanding the purpose of a governance audit.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A license audit verifies the **simultaneous presence of source identity and rights/license metadata**.

title: Reading the sequence of stages in a data governance pipeline
reading_goal: Read about the order in which provenance and rights verification are applied before the material is published.
question: What is the natural sequence of a data governance pipeline?
choices: Collection → License Verification → Processing → Save Manifest → Attribution
answer: Collection → License Verification → Processing → Save Manifest → Attribution
explanation: The `governance_flow` list specifies the sequence: collection, rights verification, provenance preservation and processing, manifest/evidence storage, and attribution publication. This is because the flow involves finalizing rights and provenance evidence before publication. A common source of confusion: Manifests and evidence are steps intended to leave a record of verification, not to hide verification results. Point of misinterpretation: This occurs when “governance traceability” is misinterpreted as “concealment.” Data governance follows the sequence: **collect → rights → provenance → evidence → attribution publish**.
project_context: It connects to a structure that manages the source, license, provenance, and submission basis of learning app data through a single release pipeline.
reading_goal_internal: 자료가 publish되기 전 provenance와 rights 검증이 어떤 순서로 적용되는지 읽는다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: The list literal enumerates the governance stages in order.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Verify that `publish` is positioned after the rights/provenance/evidence stage, not before it.
concept_explanation.key_point: Instead of publishing data immediately after collection, governance traceability is improved by verifying usage rights and documenting provenance and evidence.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: It’s easy to assume that citing sources is an optional step that can be added after publication, if necessary.

answer_explanation.step_by_step: The `governance_flow` list specifies the sequence of collection, rights verification, processing for provenance preservation, storage of manifests and evidence, and publication of attribution.
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because it is a process for confirming rights and provenance evidence prior to publication.

common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: "manifest" and "evidence" are steps taken to leave a record of verification.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: This is an example where “governance traceability” was incorrectly interpreted as “concealment.”

answer_explanation.takeaway: "Data governance" is interpreted as **collect → rights → provenance → evidence → attribution → publish**.

title: Grade whether the patch description includes implementation, behavior, and proof
reading_goal: After reading the execution of the filtered list comprehension—which adds only the row where `approved=True` to the new list of evidence—the learner concludes that a good review explanation must not only mention “adding a condition” but also connect it to the actual exclusion results and output evidence.
code:
records = [
    {"source": "portal A", "license": "CC-BY", "approved": True},
    {"source": "portal B", "license": "unknown", "approved": False},
]
submission_rows = [{"source": row["source"], "license": row["license"]} for row in records if row["approved"]]
print(submission_rows)
question: Which of the following is the most complete review description of this patch?
choices: Implementation: Filter based on the "approved" condition → Behavior: Portal B is excluded, leaving only Portal A → Evidence: The actual output contains only the single line for Portal A
The word “approved” was added to the code.
Since list comprehensions were used, all provenance issues were automatically resolved.
Since the output is a list, both performance and license compliance have been verified.
answer: Implementation: Filter based on the "approved" condition → Behavior: Portal B is excluded, leaving only Portal A → Evidence: The actual output contains only the single line for Portal A
explanation: 1) Since “approved” in the first row is True, a dict is created as a result. 2) Since “approved” in the second row is False, the resulting expression is not executed and is excluded. 3) Only the source and license for Portal A remain in `submission_rows`. 4) A good review explanation must connect the implementation (adding a condition), the behavior (excluding B), and the evidence (actual output).
project_context: Although APEX mentioned the changes, it failed to accurately explain the behavior before and after the changes and the rationale behind them; this weakness is addressed here.
reading_goal_internal: filtered list comprehension이 approved=True row만 새 근거 목록에 넣는 실행을 읽고, 좋은 리뷰 설명이 '조건 추가'뿐 아니라 실제 제외 결과와 출력 evidence까지 연결해야 함을 판단한다.

concept_explanation.what_it_is: List comprehensions with filters evaluate the condition for each item and include only those that evaluate to true in the result expression. The code review explanation must distinguish between implementation changes, observable behavioral changes, and the evidence used to verify those changes.
concept_explanation.how_to_read: Trace the `records` item by item to calculate the conditions for approval and verify the final `submission_rows`. Next, verify that the review statement includes all three elements: code changes, behavior, and execution evidence.
concept_explanation.key_point: Portal A has `approved=True`, so it remains in the result, while portal B is excluded because its value is False. Therefore, saying only “an approved filter was added” is not enough; the explanation must connect that change to evidence that only A remains in the actual result.
concept_explanation.common_mistake: If you explain a single line of code and immediately conclude that “the problem has been solved,” you may omit the actual behavior and proof.

teaching_example.code:
items = [{"name":"A","ok":True},{"name":"B","ok":False}]
kept = [item["name"] for item in items if item["ok"]]
print(kept)
teaching_example.walkthrough: "Implementation" can be explained separately as the "ok filter," "behavior" as "excluding B," and "proof" as the output ['A'].

answer_explanation.step_by_step: 1) Since “approved” in the first row is True, a dict is created as a result. 2) Since “approved” in the second row is False, the resulting expression is not executed and is excluded. 3) Only the source and license for Portal A remain in `submission_rows`. 4) A good review explanation must connect the implementation (adding a condition), the behavior (excluding B), and the evidence (actual output).
answer_explanation.why_correct: This is because it includes what the code changed, how the actual results differ, and the observed values used to verify those changes.

common_wrong_choice.choice: The word “approved” was added to the code.
common_wrong_choice.why_wrong: It only mentions implementation changes without explaining which specific rows are excluded or providing evidence to verify the results.
common_wrong_choice.misread_step: Divide the review sentence into three columns—implementation, behavior, and proof—and check for any missing columns.

answer_explanation.takeaway: A complete change description includes all three elements: **What was changed → What actually changed → How was it verified**.

target_statement: submission_rows = [{"source": row["source"], "license": row["license"]} for row in records if row["approved"]]
focus_span: [{"source": row["source"], "license": row["license"]} for row in records if row["approved"]]
reading_steps: Since “approved” in the first row is True, a dict is created.
Since `approved` in the second row is `False`, the result expression is not executed and is excluded.
Only the source and license for Portal A remain in `submission_rows`.
A good review description must connect the implementation (adding a condition), the behavior (excluding B), and the evidence (actual output).
